name: Early Blight
description: Early blight is a widespread fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani. It primarily attacks older foliage first, producing dark concentric ring lesions often called target spots.
symptoms: Small, dark brown to black spots on older leaves
Concentric rings producing a characteristic target-like pattern
Yellow halo (chlorosis) surrounding the dark lesions
Lower leaves wilt, turn completely yellow, and drop prematurely
Stem lesions with dark, sunken concentric rings
Dark leathery spots at the stem attachment point on fruit
causes: Fungal pathogen Alternaria solani overwintering in plant debris or soil
Spores splashed onto lower leaves by rain or overhead irrigation
Warm temperatures combined with heavy dew, rain, or prolonged leaf wetness
Stressed or nutrient-deficient plants are significantly more susceptible
favorableConditions: Temperatures between 24°C and 29°C (75°F–85°F) with high humidity (>90%) and leaf wetness exceeding 2 hours.
prevention: Practice 3-year crop rotation avoiding solanaceous crops (tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, eggplants)
Mulch soil around plants with clean straw or plastic to prevent spore splash from soil
Water exclusively at the base using drip irrigation or soaker hoses; avoid wetting leaves
Space plants generously to promote rapid air circulation and quick leaf drying
Select certified disease-resistant or tolerant cultivars when available
management: Prune and safely discard all infected lower foliage upon first symptom appearance (do not compost infected debris)
Stake or cage tomato vines to keep all foliage well above ground level
Clean and sanitize all pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between plants
Apply approved organic bio-fungicides such as Bacillus subtilis or copper-based preventive sprays during early onset
Ensure balanced soil nutrition, avoiding excessive nitrogen which produces overly dense susceptible foliage
disclaimer: This is a preliminary screening result. Confirm with your local agricultural extension service or certified plant pathologist before applying synthetic chemical fungicides.
sources: Cornell University Extension - Vegetable MD Online
University of California Integrated Pest Management (UC IPM) - Tomato Diseases
USDA Agricultural Research Service

name: Late Blight
description: Late blight is a devastating oomycete disease historically responsible for the Irish Potato Famine. Under cool, damp conditions it can destroy an entire field within days if unmanaged.
symptoms: Irregular water-soaked greasy gray-green lesions on leaves
Lesions rapidly expand and turn purplish-brown to black
Delicate white fuzzy fungal-like growth visible on the leaf undersides in high humidity
Dark brown, firm, sunken patches on green or ripe tomato fruit
Total collapse of foliage resembling frost damage within 3–7 days
causes: Pathogen Phytophthora infestans surviving in infected tubers or volunteer host plants
Wind-blown spores traveling miles during cloudy, humid weather
Extended periods of cool, overcast weather with free moisture on foliage
favorableConditions: Cool, humid weather: temperatures between 15°C and 22°C (60°F–72°F) accompanied by relative humidity above 90% for more than 10 hours.
prevention: Plant only certified disease-free transplants and certified seed potatoes
Eradicate volunteer tomato and potato plants near planting beds
Avoid overhead irrigation, especially in early morning or evening hours
Monitor regional pest alerts for late blight outbreaks in your area
management: Immediately rogue (pull out) and bag heavily infected plants; do not compost
Protect neighboring healthy rows with preventive bio-fungicides or copper compounds
Destroy infected crop residues immediately after harvest
Alert neighboring growers as late blight spores are airborne and spread rapidly
disclaimer: Late blight is a community-level agricultural emergency. Notify your local agricultural advisory officer promptly upon confirmed observation.
sources: USDA Plant Disease Diagnostic Laboratory
Penn State Extension - Tomato Late Blight Guide
North Carolina State University Extension

name: Healthy Tomato
description: The leaf appears vigorous, well-pigmented, and free from visible signs of infectious lesions, powdery mildew, or pest infestations.
symptoms: Even deep-green coloration across leaf surfaces
Crisp, erect leaf texture without wilting or curling
Absence of necrotic spots, halos, lesions, or fungal mycelium
Clean stem and leaf petiole attachment points
causes: Optimal balance of sunlight, soil moisture, and essential plant macronutrients
Good soil drainage and adequate root aeration
Effective preventive hygiene and pest management practices
favorableConditions: 6–8 hours of direct daily sunlight, well-draining loamy soil with pH 6.2–6.8, consistent base-level watering.
prevention: Maintain consistent soil moisture without waterlogging
Provide organic mulch around base to conserve water and prevent soil splash
Fertilize with balanced tomato fertilizer containing calcium to prevent blossom end rot
Inspect leaves weekly, particularly lower foliage, for earliest signs of stress
management: Continue regular cultural care and routine scouting
Prune bottom suckers touching the ground to maximize airflow
No chemical or therapeutic intervention is necessary
disclaimer: Visual health does not preclude early microscopic pathogen incubation or subterranean root issues. Regular monitoring remains recommended.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society - Tomato Cultivation Guide
University of Florida IFAS Extension

name: Bacterial Spot
description: Bacterial spot is caused by several Xanthomonas species. It attacks leaves, stems, and fruits, significantly reducing yield and marketable fruit quality during warm, wet seasons.
symptoms: Small (under 3mm), dark brown to black circular lesions with greasy or water-soaked borders
Lesions may have a faint yellow halo and angular appearance confined by leaf veins
Centers of lesions frequently dry up, crack, and tear out leaving shot-hole perforations
Foliage blights, turns brown, and defoliates rapidly during persistent rain
Raised scabby black blister-like spots on green fruit
causes: Bacterial seed contamination or infected greenhouse transplant seedlings
Rain splashes, overhead sprinklers, and handling wet foliage during field operations
Bacteria enter leaf stomata and natural openings or wound sites caused by wind/insects
favorableConditions: Warm (24°C–30°C / 75°F–85°F), wet, rainy weather, and prolonged high relative humidity.
prevention: Always source certified, hot-water treated pathogen-free seeds
Avoid handling or cultivating tomato plants when leaves are wet with dew or rain
Rotate fields away from solanaceous crops for at least two years
Implement drip irrigation to keep canopy completely dry
management: Prune out early infected leaf branches using sterilized shears
Apply preventive copper bactericide combined with mancozeb if recommended by local extension
Remove and destroy crop residues immediately at the end of the harvest season
disclaimer: Bacterial spot does not respond to standard fungal medications. Antibiotics should only be used if legally registered for agricultural use in your jurisdiction.
sources: University of Florida IFAS - Bacterial Spot Management
Ohio State University Extension Fact Sheet

name: Leaf Mold
description: Leaf mold predominantly impacts tomatoes cultivated in high tunnels, greenhouses, and humid sheltered microclimates with stagnant airflow.
symptoms: Pale green to yellowish indistinct patches on upper leaf surfaces
Olive-green to velvety brown mold growth directly underneath the yellow spots on leaf undersides
Infected leaves gradually curl, wither, turn brown, and drop off
In severe cases, blossoms and stems are blighted
causes: Fungal spores remaining viable in greenhouse structures and plant debris for months
Prolonged relative humidity (>85%) combined with warm greenhouse temperatures
Dense, unpruned canopies restricting airflow
favorableConditions: Temperatures between 21°C and 24°C (70°F–75°F) with high relative humidity (>85%).
prevention: Provide active greenhouse ventilation with exhaust fans and horizontal airflow fans
Keep night temperatures warm enough to prevent condensation on foliage
Prune suckers and stake plants to maintain an open canopy
management: Strip lower infected leaves promptly
Increase heat and ventilation to lower greenhouse relative humidity below 80%
Apply protective bio-fungicides or registered fungicides if disease pressure is high
disclaimer: Ensure proper protective equipment when applying any treatment inside enclosed greenhouse environments.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension - Tomato Leaf Mold
Rutgers NJAES Plant Pathology

name: Septoria Leaf Spot
description: A very common fungal foliar disease that starts on lower leaves after fruit set, causing extensive premature defoliation which leads to sunscald on unprotected fruit.
symptoms: Numerous small circular spots (1.5–3 mm) on lower foliage
Distinct dark brown borders with light tan or gray centers
Tiny black specks (pycnidia fruiting bodies) visible in the spot center with a magnifying glass
Leaves turn completely yellow, wither, and fall, progressing upward through the canopy
causes: Septoria lycopersici surviving in overwintered solanaceous weeds (horsenettle) and crop debris
Water droplets splashing fungal spores from the soil surface to lower leaves
favorableConditions: Warm weather (20°C–25°C / 68°F–77°F) with high humidity, heavy dew, or prolonged rainfall.
prevention: Apply 5–7 cm layer of clean mulch beneath plants to eliminate soil splash
Maintain a 2- to 3-year crop rotation schedule
Eliminate solanaceous weeds around garden perimeter
Water exclusively via drip tape at soil level
management: Remove infected bottom foliage immediately upon notice
Sanitize pruning tools between cuts with rubbing alcohol
Apply preventive copper or bio-fungicide treatments to preserve upper foliage
disclaimer: Septoria primarily impacts leaves rather than fruit directly, but defoliation exposes fruit to severe sunscald.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden - Septoria Leaf Spot
University of Wisconsin-Madison Extension

name: Target Spot
description: Target spot is a fungal disease that thrives in tropical and subtropical climates, affecting leaves, stems, and fruit with distinctive concentric lesions.
symptoms: Small pinpoint brown flecks on upper leaf surfaces expanding into circular lesions
Lesions with light brown centers, dark brown borders, and subtle concentric rings
Leaves turn yellow and fall off prematurely
Sunken crater-like spots on tomato fruits with cracked centers
causes: Corynespora cassiicola fungus persisting in infected crop residues and weed hosts
Airborne spores dispersed by wind and rain splash in humid conditions
favorableConditions: Temperatures around 20°C–28°C with prolonged humidity above 80% and long leaf wetness duration.
prevention: Promote good air movement through adequate vine spacing and pruning
Rotate out of solanaceous crops for minimum 2 years
Clear all infected plant material after harvest
management: Remove severely spotted leaves
Ensure proper irrigation timing to avoid overnight leaf wetness
Apply registered protective fungicides early in disease development
disclaimer: Can be confused with Early Blight; accurate laboratory confirmation may be helpful in commercial settings.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension - Target Spot of Tomato
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension

name: Tomato Mosaic Virus
description: Tomato mosaic virus is an extremely stable, easily transmitted plant virus that causes mottling, distorted foliage, and stunted vegetative growth.
symptoms: Mottling of alternating light and dark green areas on leaves ('mosaic' pattern)
Distorted, blistered, crinkled, or strap-like leaves (fern-leaf effect)
Stunted overall plant growth and reduced fruit yield
Uneven fruit ripening with internal brown necrotic rings
causes: Mechanical transmission through touch, contaminated gardening tools, stakes, and hands
Virus particles can persist on seed coats, dried tobacco products, and dried plant debris for years
Not primarily transmitted by insect vectors; mechanical contact is chief route
favorableConditions: Can occur at any temperature where tomatoes grow; symptoms are most visible during rapid vegetative growth.
prevention: Choose certified virus-resistant varieties (labeled 'TMV' or 'ToMV' resistant)
Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water after handling tobacco products before touching plants
Disinfect stakes, trellises, and garden tools in 10% household bleach or virucidal solution
Use only certified virus-free seed stock
management: There is no cure for virally infected plants; rogue and discard affected plants immediately
Do not compost infected plants; burn or seal in trash bags
Sanitize all tools, gloves, and containers thoroughly before moving to healthy plants
disclaimer: Chemical sprays (fungicides, bactericides) have zero efficacy against plant viruses.
sources: University of California IPM - Tomato Mosaic Virus
Penn State Extension - Plant Virus Management

name: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus
description: TYLCV is a begomovirus transmitted by silverleaf whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci). It is one of the most economically damaging tomato viruses in warm and subtropical zones.
symptoms: Severe upward curling and cupping of leaflet margins
Prominent marginal and interveinal yellowing (chlorosis)
Pronounced plant stunting and erect bushy appearance
Complete flower drop resulting in total failure to set fruit if infected early
causes: Exclusively transmitted by the silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci)
Weed reservoirs and infected alternate host crops (peppers, tobacco, weeds)
Not mechanically transmitted through sap or gardening tools
favorableConditions: Warm dry environments where whitefly populations explode rapidly; high temperatures (25°C–35°C).
prevention: Plant TYLCV-resistant hybrid tomato cultivars
Use fine mesh insect netting (50-mesh) in nurseries and high tunnels to exclude whiteflies
Install yellow sticky traps to monitor and reduce whitefly adult populations
Eradicate nightshade and mallow weeds near the crop area
management: Pull and dispose of infected plants showing severe stunting to reduce viral reservoir
Control whitefly vectors using insecticidal soaps, horticultural oils, or neem products
Cover newly transplanted seedlings with floating row covers until flowering begins
disclaimer: Infection before flowering often leads to 100% yield loss on that specimen. Early whitefly vector control is essential.
sources: UC Davis IPM - Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl
CABI Invasive Species Compendium - TYLCV

name: Early Blight
description: Early blight in potatoes affects older leaves, stems, and tubers, leading to premature foliage loss and reduced tuber sizing and storage quality.
symptoms: Dark brown to black angular lesions with concentric target rings
Yellowing of leaf tissue surrounding older lesions
Premature leaf senescence starting from lower canopy upward
Tubers develop sunken, dark, leathery lesions with raised margins during storage
causes: Alternaria solani overwintering in unharvested cull potatoes, volunteer tubers, or crop residue
Splattering rainfall and overhead irrigation dispersing fungal conidia onto lower foliage
favorableConditions: Alternating wet and dry periods with temperatures around 20°C–25°C.
prevention: Plant only certified seed potatoes free from blemishes and rot
Practice 3- to 4-year crop rotations with non-solanaceous crops (grasses, brassicas)
Ensure adequate nitrogen and potassium fertility; deficient plants succumb earlier
Allow tubers to fully mature and skin-set before harvest
management: Avoid wounding potato tubers during harvest and handling
Cure harvested potatoes at 10°C–15°C with high humidity for 2 weeks to heal minor abrasions
Destroy potato vines 2–3 weeks before harvesting to reduce tuber spore contact
disclaimer: Store potatoes in clean, ventilated, cool storage; cull any rotten tubers immediately.
sources: International Potato Center (CIP)
University of Idaho Extension - Potato Pathology

name: Late Blight
description: The catastrophic disease that caused the 1840s European Potato Famine. It rapidly rots potato foliage and penetrates tubers, causing dry or wet rot.
symptoms: Dark, water-soaked, irregular lesions expanding rapidly across foliage
White moldy mildew visible on undersides of leaves during humid mornings
Foliage blackens, wilts, and gives off a characteristic pungent odor
Tubers show coppery brown or purplish sunken surface skin and reddish-brown dry granular rot internally
causes: Infected seed tubers or volunteer tubers surviving winter in soil or cull piles
Airborne sporangia carried on damp winds for miles
favorableConditions: Cool, overcast, humid days (15°C–20°C) with persistent leaf wetness >10 hours.
prevention: Plant certified seed tubers from inspected disease-free sources
Eliminate all cull piles and volunteer potatoes in the surrounding vicinity
Hill soil generously around potato hills to prevent spores washing into the tuber zone
Apply preventive fungicides before canopy closure if regional disease forecasts indicate high risk
management: Kill potato vines completely at least 2 weeks before harvest using mechanical mowing or approved desiccant
Never harvest potatoes in wet soil or rainy weather
Inspect stored potatoes regularly and immediately discard decomposing tubers
disclaimer: Late blight is federally and regionally monitored in many agricultural districts. Report severe suspected outbreaks.
sources: European Association for Potato Research
Cornell University Late Blight Monitoring Network

name: Healthy Potato
description: Vigorous, healthy potato foliage displaying uniform green pigment, robust leaf turgidity, and no evidence of fungal, bacterial, or viral pathogen infection.
symptoms: Deep green, lush foliage with uniform leaf margins
No spots, necrotic margins, water-soaking, or powdery coatings
Sturdy erect stems supporting healthy canopy structure
causes: Quality seed stock, balanced soil nutrition, and proper hill mounding
Consistent moisture management preventing drought stress and waterlogging
favorableConditions: Full sun, loose well-drained acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.5), cool root zone conditions.
prevention: Hill potatoes progressively as stems grow to prevent green tubers and spore wash
Keep soil evenly moist especially during flowering and tuber bulking
Perform regular scouting for Colorado potato beetles and foliar spots
management: Maintain routine agricultural care; no chemical interventions required
Ensure proper irrigation schedule
disclaimer: Field surveillance should be maintained through harvest to detect late-season pathogen emergence.
sources: Purdue University Extension - Potato Production
Michigan State University Potato Diagnostic Guide

name: Bacterial Spot
description: A serious bacterial disease of peppers causing defoliation, blossom drop, and severely scarred fruit, reducing yield drastically in warm, humid regions.
symptoms: Small, circular to irregular water-soaked spots on leaf undersides
Spots turn purplish-brown to black with pale brownish centers on the upper leaf surface
Severe yellowing of foliage surrounding lesions and sudden leaf drop leaving bare stems
Rough, raised, warty brown lesions on pepper fruits
causes: Contaminated pepper seeds or infected greenhouse transplants
Bacteria spread by splashing rain, overhead irrigation, and farm machinery
Entry through stomata and leaf injuries
favorableConditions: Warm weather (24°C–30°C / 75°F–86°F) combined with frequent rain or high humidity.
prevention: Plant certified disease-free, tested seed lots or resistant bell pepper cultivars (races 1-10 resistant)
Strictly avoid overhead irrigation; use drip lines at the soil surface
Do not enter fields or touch pepper plants when foliage is wet
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops for 2 or more years
management: Apply protective copper-mancozeb tank mixes as recommended by regional extension
Rogue out severely diseased seedling flats in the nursery immediately
Incorporate plant residues thoroughly after harvest to accelerate bacterial decomposition
disclaimer: Copper-tolerant bacterial strains are common; consult your county extension agent for effective regional bactericides.
sources: Rutgers Cooperative Extension - Pepper Bacterial Spot
University of Georgia Plant Pathology

name: Healthy Bell Pepper
description: The bell pepper foliage exhibits lush green color, firm glossy leaves, strong branch nodes, and no symptoms of pathogenic infection or nutritional deficiency.
symptoms: Glossy, uniform emerald-green leaf surface
Intact smooth leaf margins without curling or warty spots
Strong erect branch nodes with healthy flower buds
causes: Optimal soil warmth, balanced phosphorus/potassium nutrition, and careful irrigation
Proactive pest management keeping aphid and thrips vectors at bay
favorableConditions: Warm sunny days (21°C–29°C), night temperatures above 15°C, well-drained fertile soil with pH 6.0–6.8.
prevention: Provide consistent irrigation to prevent blossom end rot and calcium deficiency
Support heavy pepper branches with stakes or cages to prevent ground contact
Mulch soil surface to conserve moisture and suppress weeds
management: Continue standard cultural practices and weekly scouting
No therapeutic treatment needed
disclaimer: Monitor fruit development for calcium deficiency (blossom end rot) during sudden hot spells.
sources: University of California Davis - Pepper Production Guide
Clemson Cooperative Extension

name: Common Rust
description: Common rust is caused by the obligate fungus Puccinia sorghi. It produces characteristic powdery cinnamon-brown pustules on both upper and lower corn leaf surfaces.
symptoms: Oval to elongate cinnamon-brown pustules (uredinia) scattered over both leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture the epidermis, releasing powdery reddish-brown spores that rub off on fingers
As plants mature, pustules turn brownish-black as winter teliospores develop
Severe rust leads to leaf chlorosis, death, and poor ear filling
causes: Fungal spores carried northward on storm winds from warmer southern regions
Cool to moderate temperatures paired with high humidity and morning dews
favorableConditions: Temperatures of 16°C–24°C (60°F–75°F) with high relative humidity (>95%) and 6+ hours of dew.
prevention: Plant rust-resistant corn hybrids (with Rp genes)
Plant early in the season to allow corn to mature before airborne rust spore loads peak
Ensure balanced soil fertilization
management: Foliar fungicides may be justified if rust pustules cover more than 10-15% of the leaf surface before tasseling
Post-tasseling fungicide applications are rarely cost-effective in field corn
disclaimer: Common rust must be distinguished from Southern Rust (Puccinia polysora), which is more aggressive at high temperatures.
sources: Iowa State University Extension - Corn Diseases
Purdue Field Crop Pathology

name: Healthy Corn
description: Healthy maize foliage featuring wide, upright, emerald-green leaves with clear venation, robust stalks, and no fungal pustules or blight streaks.
symptoms: Vibrant uniform green color across broad leaf blades
Smooth leaf margins free from lesions, rust dust, or striping
Strong stalk whorl and vigorous vegetative development
causes: Adequate soil nitrogen, full sunlight exposure, and regular moisture availability
Proper planting depth and soil drainage preventing root asphyxiation
favorableConditions: Full sun, soil temperatures above 15°C at planting, warm growing season, deep loamy soil.
prevention: Apply nitrogen split-applications matching corn vegetative uptake stages
Maintain weed-free rows during critical early growth stages (V1–V6)
Scout for corn earworm and armyworms during silking
management: Maintain standard agronomic care; no chemical treatments required
disclaimer: Regularly check leaf collar stages and moisture status during critical tasseling and silking periods.
sources: Purdue University Corn Production Guide
University of Illinois Crop Sciences

name: Apple Scab
description: Apple scab is the most ubiquitous and economically serious disease of apples and flowering crabapples worldwide, causing olive-green velvety lesions on leaves and corky scabs on fruit.
symptoms: Velvety, olive-green to dark brown circular spots on leaf surfaces
Lesions become raised and puckered with distinct feathery margins
Infected leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely, causing early summer defoliation
Fruit develops dark, scabby, corky spots that crack as the apple grows, allowing secondary rots
causes: Venturia inaequalis fungus overwintering in fallen dead leaves on the orchard floor
Spring ascospores released during rain events matching the Mills infection period table
favorableConditions: Cool, wet spring weather (13°C–24°C / 55°F–75°F) with leaf wetness persisting for 6 to 28 hours.
prevention: Rake, chop, or flail-mow fallen apple leaves in autumn or apply urea spray to accelerate leaf breakdown
Prune apple tree canopies open in late winter to facilitate rapid sun drying and air circulation
Plant scab-resistant cultivars such as Liberty, Prima, Freedom, or Enterprise
management: Apply protective preventive bio-fungicides or sulfur sprays beginning at green tip and through petal fall
Thin diseased fruit early to redirect tree resources into healthy fruitlets
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation in the orchard canopy
disclaimer: Once scab lesions are visible on leaves, chemical eradicant options are limited; prevention is key.
sources: Cornell Fruit Resources - Apple Scab Management
University of Massachusetts Amherst Extension

name: Black Rot (Frogeye Leaf Spot)
description: Black rot attacks apple leaves (known as frogeye leaf spot), branches (cankers), and ripening fruit, producing firm decaying concentric dark rings.
symptoms: Frogeye leaf spots: small purple spots expanding into circular lesions with light brown centers and dark purple halos
Small black fungal fruiting bodies (pycnidia) in the spot centers
Sunken, reddish-brown bark cankers on branches and limbs
Fruit rot begins at the calyx end with concentric alternating light and dark brown rings, rotting into a firm black mummified apple
causes: Botryosphaeria obtusa surviving in dead wood, branch cankers, fire-blight strikes, and mummified fruit left on trees
Rain splashes dispersing spores to foliage and fruit wounds
favorableConditions: Warm (20°C–27°C / 68°F–80°F) and wet periods during and after blossom.
prevention: Prune out all dead wood, cankered limbs, and winter mummies during dormant pruning
Disinfect pruning saws between trees
Burn or chop and remove all orchard prunings away from the trees
management: Prune 15 cm below any visible bark canker into healthy wood
Maintain preventive foliar protection from petal fall through harvest
disclaimer: Removing source cankers and mummies is the single most critical cultural control.
sources: Penn State Extension - Apple Black Rot
Virginia Tech Fruit Pathology

name: Cedar Apple Rust
description: A heteroecious rust fungus requiring two distinct host species—apple/crabapple and Eastern red cedar/juniper—to complete its complex life cycle.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange or reddish-yellow circular spots on upper apple leaf surfaces
Tiny black dots (pycnia) appearing inside the center of yellow leaf spots
Tube-like or fringe-like spore structures (aecia) protruding from the underside of the leaf directly below the spots
Fruit may develop raised, orange spots near the calyx end
causes: Spores blown from gelatinous orange horn-like galls on nearby juniper/red cedar trees during spring rain
Cannot spread directly from apple leaf to apple leaf
favorableConditions: Wet spring periods between 10°C and 24°C coinciding with apple pink bud through petal fall.
prevention: Remove Eastern red cedar trees located within several hundred meters of the apple orchard where feasible
Prune out brown woody galls on ornamental junipers in late winter before spring rains
Select rust-immune or resistant apple cultivars such as Redfree, Liberty, or Freedom
management: Apply protective fungicides to apple foliage starting at pink bud stage if junipers are nearby
Treatment after lesions appear on apple leaves will not eradicate existing spots
disclaimer: If no juniper or red cedar hosts exist in the area, the disease cycle is completely severed.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension - Cedar Apple Rust
West Virginia University Extension

name: Healthy Apple
description: Healthy apple foliage with thick leathery green leaves, intact serrated margins, clean leaf undersides, and vigorous fruit spur development.
symptoms: Uniform medium-to-deep green leaf pigmentation
Crisp serrated leaf edges without curling, chlorosis, or necrotic spots
Absence of powdery mildew coats, warty spots, or rust pustules
causes: Proper annual pruning allowing adequate sunlight penetration throughout the canopy
Well-drained soil, adequate calcium and boron availability, and sound pest management
favorableConditions: Full sun, cold winter chilling requirements fulfilled, well-drained loamy soil pH 6.0–7.0.
prevention: Perform annual dormant pruning to thin dense interior tree branches
Maintain a mulch ring around the tree base keeping grass away from the trunk
Monitor for codling moth, aphids, and mites
management: Continue seasonal orchard care; no pathogen spray necessary
disclaimer: Ensure regular checks of fruit development and monitor for seasonal insect pests.
sources: Cornell University Orchard Management Guide
Washington State University Tree Fruit Research

name: Powdery Mildew
description: Powdery mildew is one of the most recognizable plant diseases, manifesting as talcum powder-like white or gray fungal patches across leaves, stems, and buds on a wide range of plants.
symptoms: White to grayish powdery fungal patches on upper leaf surfaces and young shoots
Leaves may twist, buckle, distort, or cup upward
Infected leaves gradually turn yellow, brown, and dry out prematurely
Stunted flower and fruit growth with surface blemishes
causes: Specialized powdery mildew fungal species whose airborne conidia do not require free water to germinate
Warm dry days followed by cool humid nights
favorableConditions: Temperatures between 15°C and 27°C with high relative humidity at night (70%), but dry daytime leaf surfaces.
prevention: Plant in full sun; powdery mildew fungi prefer shady, sheltered areas
Provide generous spacing between plants to maximize airflow
Choose resistant vegetable and ornamental varieties
management: Prune crowded shoots to allow sunlight penetration
Apply potassium bicarbonate, horticultural neem oil, or sulfur-based sprays at the earliest sign
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which stimulates vulnerable tender growth
disclaimer: Educational record only. Not in current mobile vision model supported classes.
sources: University of California IPM - Powdery Mildew on Vegetables
Royal Horticultural Society

name: Downy Mildew
description: Downy mildew is an aggressive water mold pathogen that causes angular yellow patches bounded by leaf veins on the upper surface and purplish-gray downy mold underneath.
symptoms: Bright angular yellow lesions strictly delimited by major leaf veins on upper leaf surface
Purplish, grayish, or brown downy felt visible on the corresponding leaf undersides in morning dew
Rapid browning and crisping of foliage causing complete canopy defoliation
causes: Oomycete pathogen spread on wind currents from warmer overwintering zones
Requires free moisture on leaves for swimming zoospores to infect
favorableConditions: Cool to moderate temperatures (15°C–20°C) with persistent moisture, rain, or heavy fog.
prevention: Grow crops using drip irrigation and avoid wetting leaves
Space plants widely and train vines on trellises
Select downy mildew-resistant hybrids
management: Remove infected plants immediately to prevent neighborhood spread
Apply targeted preventive copper or specialized oomycete fungicides
disclaimer: Educational record only. Not in current mobile vision model supported classes.
sources: Cucurbit Downy Mildew Forecasting System
NC State Extension

name: Blossom End Rot (Abiotic)
description: A physiological, non-infectious disorder caused by an localized calcium deficiency in developing fruit tissue, almost always triggered by inconsistent soil moisture.
symptoms: Water-soaked spot at the blossom end (bottom) of green fruit
Spot enlarges, turns dark brown to black, and becomes sunken and leathery
Foliage typically remains completely healthy and green
Affected fruit ripens prematurely
causes: Fluctuating soil moisture (cycling between drought and saturated conditions)
Excessive nitrogen fertilizer (especially ammonium-based) inhibiting calcium uptake
Soil calcium deficiency or high soil salinity/pH imbalance
Rapid early vegetative growth outstripping root calcium transport
favorableConditions: Hot, dry, windy weather causing high transpiration rates, combined with erratic watering.
prevention: Maintain consistent, even soil moisture with mulch and drip irrigation
Conduct soil testing; amend acidic soil with agricultural lime to maintain pH 6.2–6.8
Avoid deep cultivation near root systems to prevent root pruning
Avoid excessive high-nitrogen fertilizers during fruit set
management: Remove affected fruit so the plant redirects calcium and energy to subsequent blossoms
Regulate irrigation timer to provide steady, even moisture
Foliar calcium sprays offer limited temporary relief; soil moisture regulation is primary solution
disclaimer: Non-infectious disorder. Do NOT apply fungicides or bactericides.
sources: UC Davis Vegetable Research and Information Center
University of Georgia Extension

name: Nitrogen Deficiency (Abiotic)
description: Nitrogen is a mobile macronutrient required for chlorophyll synthesis. Deficiency causes older lower leaves to turn pale green to yellow first as the plant remobilizes nitrogen to new growth.
symptoms: General pale green to yellowing (chlorosis) beginning uniformly on the oldest lower leaves
Yellowing progresses gradually upward through the canopy if uncorrected
Stunted vegetative growth and thin spindly stems
Small, pale leaves and reduced flower/fruit production
causes: Low soil organic matter or leaching of nitrates by excessive heavy rains
Waterlogged, compacted soil hindering root nutrient absorption
Cold soil temperatures slowing microbial nitrogen mineralization
favorableConditions: Sandy soils low in organic matter or soils experiencing prolonged heavy rainfall.
prevention: Incorporate well-composted organic matter or aged manure before planting
Plant nitrogen-fixing cover crops (clover, vetch, peas) in crop rotation
Avoid overwatering that leaches soluble nutrients below the root zone
management: Apply balanced organic fertilizer (fish emulsion, blood meal) or balanced soluble plant food
Maintain healthy soil microbial activity with compost teas and organic mulch
disclaimer: Non-infectious physiological symptom. Easily corrected with balanced organic fertilization.
sources: FAO Soil Fertility and Plant Nutrition Guide
International Plant Nutrition Institute
